claim: RIF1 functions in the 53BP1-Shieldin pathway that inhibits resection of DNA ends during repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs).
source: During repair of DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), RIF1 functions in the 53BP1-Shieldin pathway that inhibits resection of DNA ends to modulate the cellular decision on which repair pathway to engage.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work establishing this pathway.

claim: Under conditions of replication stress, RIF1 protects nascent DNA at stalled replication forks from degradation by the DNA2 nuclease.
source: Under conditions of replication stress, RIF1 protects nascent DNA at stalled replication forks from degradation by the DNA2 nuclease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: A cluster of conserved ATM/ATR consensus SQ motifs within the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of mouse RIF1 are phosphorylated in proliferating B lymphocytes.
source: Here, we identified a cluster of conserved ATM/ATR consensus SQ motifs within the intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of mouse RIF1 that are phosphorylated in proliferating B lymphocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data presented in the manuscript (Figure 1E and F).

claim: Phosphorylation of the conserved IDR SQ cluster is dispensable for the inhibition of DSB resection by RIF1.
source: We found that phosphorylation of the conserved IDR SQ cluster is dispensable for the inhibition of DSB resection by RIF1, but is essential to counteract DNA2-dependent degradation of nascent DNA at stalled replication forks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing that RIF1 S→A mutants retain DSB end protection function (Figure 2G-I, Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).

claim: Phosphorylation of the conserved IDR SQ cluster is essential to counteract DNA2-dependent degradation of nascent DNA at stalled replication forks.
source: We found that phosphorylation of the conserved IDR SQ cluster is dispensable for the inhibition of DSB resection by RIF1, but is essential to counteract DNA2-dependent degradation of nascent DNA at stalled replication forks.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data showing fork degradation in RIF1 S→A mutants (Figure 3C, D).

claim: Extensive 5′ to 3′ resection of DSBs inhibits repair by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) but is a prerequisite for homology-dependent repair processes.
source: Extensive 5′ to 3′ resection of DSBs inhibits repair by nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) but is a prerequisite for homology-dependent repair processes (homologous recombination [HR] and alternative end joining [A-EJ]) (Chang et al., 2017; Symington, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Dysregulated DSB end processing can lead to unproductive or aberrant repair reactions with dramatic consequences at both cellular and systemic levels.
source: As a result, dysregulated DSB end processing can lead to unproductive or aberrant repair reactions with dramatic consequences at both cellular and systemic levels, as evidenced during repair of programmed DSBs in B lymphocytes undergoing class switch recombination (CSR) and of stochastic DNA replication-associated breaks in BRCA1-mutated cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and established knowledge.

claim: Immunoglobulin (Ig) CSR is the process occurring in mature B lymphocytes that enables the formation of different Ig classes or isotypes.
source: Immunoglobulin (Ig) CSR is the process occurring in mature B lymphocytes that enables the formation of different Ig classes or isotypes, thus diversifying the effector component of immune responses (Methot and Di Noia, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CSR is mediated by a deletional recombination reaction at the Ig heavy chain locus (Igh) that replaces the constant (C) gene for the basal IgM isotype with one of the downstream C genes encoding a different Ig class.
source: At the molecular level, CSR is mediated by a deletional recombination reaction at the Ig heavy chain locus (Igh) that replaces the constant (C) gene for the basal IgM isotype with one of the downstream C genes encoding a different Ig class (Yewdell and Chaudhuri, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The CSR reaction is initiated by the formation of multiple programmed DSBs at internally repetitive DNA stretches, known as switch (S) regions, preceding the recombining C regions.
source: The reaction is initiated by the formation of multiple programmed DSBs at internally repetitive DNA stretches, known as switch (S) regions, preceding the recombining C regions (Saha et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Productive CSR events occur via protection of DSBs from nucleolytic resection, which enables NHEJ-mediated inter-S-region repair.
source: Productive CSR events occur via protection of DSBs from nucleolytic resection, which enables NHEJ-mediated inter-S-region repair (Boboila et al., 2012; Saha et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Defects in DSB end protection lead to unscheduled processing of S region breaks, which favors local, unproductive, intra-S-region recombination reactions, and results in immunodeficiency.
source: Defects in DSB end protection lead to unscheduled processing of S region breaks, which, combined with the close break proximity and the repetitive nature of these DNA stretches, favors local, hence unproductive, intra-S-region recombination reactions, and results in immunodeficiency (Boersma et al., 2015; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Findlay et al., 2018; Ghezraoui et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2018; Hakim et al., 2012; Ling et al., 2020; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Panchakshari et al., 2018; Reina-San-Martin et al., 2007; Xu et al., 2015; Yamane et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Extensive processing is essential for repair of DNA replication-associated breaks, which employs HR as the physiological repair pathway.
source: Conversely, extensive processing is essential for repair of DNA replication-associated breaks, which employs HR as the physiological repair pathway (Scully et al., 2019; Symington, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The HR protein BRCA1 specifically counteracts DSB end protection, thus enabling resection and HR.
source: In this context, the HR protein BRCA1 specifically counteracts DSB end protection, thus enabling resection and HR (Bunting et al., 2010; Tarsounas and Sung, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Absence of BRCA1 causes persistent protection of DNA replication-associated DSBs, which interferes with their physiological repair by HR.
source: Absence of BRCA1 causes persistent protection of DNA replication-associated DSBs, which interferes with their physiological repair by HR (Bunting et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: BRCA1-mutated cells accumulate unrepaired DSBs and aberrant NHEJ-mediated chromosome fusions known as radials.
source: As a result, cells accumulate unrepaired DSBs and aberrant NHEJ-mediated chromosome fusions known as radials (Bouwman et al., 2010; Bunting et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The increased levels of genome instability are responsible for the lethality of BRCA1-mutated cells and mouse models.
source: The increased levels of genome instability are responsible for the lethality of BRCA1-mutated cells and mouse models (Tarsounas and Sung, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Defects in DSB end protection can relieve the inhibitory brake on resection in BRCA1-mutated cells and partially rescue HR, genome stability, and viability.
source: Defects in DSB end protection can relieve the inhibitory brake on resection in BRCA1-mutated cells and partially rescue HR, genome stability, and viability (Bouwman et al., 2010; Bunting et al., 2010; Cao et al., 2009; Chapman et al., 2013; Dev et al., 2018; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Findlay et al., 2018; Ghezraoui et al., 2018; Gupta et al., 2018; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2015; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Pathways that counteract the nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA at replication forks are crucial to maintain genome stability under conditions of replication stress.
source: Recently, pathways that counteract the nucleolytic degradation of nascent DNA at replication forks have proven to be crucial to maintain genome stability under conditions of replication stress (Pasero and Vindigni, 2017; Rickman and Smogorzewska, 2019; Schlacher et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Replication fork reversal is the mechanism that converts a classic three-way junction fork into a four-way junction structure via the annealing of the newly synthesized complementary DNA strands and the re-annealing of the parental strands.
source: Replication fork reversal is the mechanism that converts a classic three-way junction fork into a four-way junction structure via the annealing of the newly synthesized complementary DNA strands and the re-annealing of the parental strands (Neelsen and Lopes, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Replication fork reversal appears to have a stabilizing effect on forks stalled as a consequence of DNA replication stress.
source: This process, which results in the formation of a fourth regressed arm, appears to have a stabilizing effect on forks stalled as a consequence of DNA replication stress (Liao et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Reversed forks can act as the entry point for various DNA nucleases, and unrestrained processing of the newly replicated DNA in the absence of protective factors leads to accumulation of DNA breaks and hypersensitivity to replication stress-inducing agents.
source: However, reversed forks can act as the entry point for various DNA nucleases, and unrestrained processing of the newly replicated DNA in the absence of protective factors leads to accumulation of DNA breaks and hypersensitivity to replication stress-inducing agents (Cortez, 2015; Neelsen and Lopes, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: During repair of DSBs, RIF1 acts in the 53BP1/Shieldin-mediated cascade that inhibits resection of DNA ends.
source: During repair of DSBs, RIF1 acts in the 53BP1/Shieldin-mediated cascade that inhibits resection of DNA ends (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Ablation of RIF1 in mature B cells severely impairs NHEJ repair of CSR DSBs and leads to immunodeficiency in mouse models.
source: As a consequence, ablation of RIF1 in mature B cells severely impairs NHEJ repair of CSR DSBs and leads to immunodeficiency in mouse models (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of RIF1 in BRCA1-deficient cells partially restores resection and HR-dependent repair of DNA replication-associated breaks, and reduces genome instability and cell lethality.
source: Conversely, deletion of RIF1 in BRCA1-deficient cells partially restores resection and HR-dependent repair of DNA replication-associated breaks, and reduces genome instability and cell lethality of this genetic background (Chapman et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RIF1 is recruited to stalled DNA replication forks and protects newly synthesized DNA from processing by the DNA2 nuclease.
source: RIF1 is recruited to stalled DNA replication forks and protects newly synthesized DNA from processing by the DNA2 nuclease (Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Loss of RIF1 leads to increased degradation of nascent DNA at reversed forks and exposure of under-replicated DNA and genome instability.
source: Loss of RIF1 leads to increased degradation of nascent DNA at reversed forks and exposure of under-replicated DNA and genome instability (Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016; Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: RIF1 is a large protein of almost 2500 amino acids in mammalian cells with no known enzymatic activity.
source: RIF1 is a large protein of almost 2500 amino acids in mammalian cells (Figure 1—source data 1) with no known enzymatic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to source data and established knowledge.

claim: Two motifs are highly conserved in RIF1 homologs from yeast to mammals: the N-terminal HEAT repeats, and the SILK-RVxF motif.
source: While information about RIF1 structural organization is limited, analyses of RIF1 homologs across species identified two motifs that are highly conserved from yeast to mammals: the N-terminal Huntingtin, Elongation factor 3, A subunit of protein phosphatase 2A, and Tor1 (HEAT) repeats, and the SILK-RVxF motif, whose sequence location shifted from the N-terminus to the C-terminal end during the evolution of unicellular to multicellular organisms (Figure 1A; Sreesankar et al., 2012; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and Figure 1A.

claim: In vertebrates, RIF1 exhibits a conserved C-terminal domain with a tripartite structure.
source: In vertebrates, RIF1 also exhibits a conserved C-terminal domain with a tripartite structure (Figure 1A; Xu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and Figure 1A.

claim: The region spanning between the N- and C-terminal motifs of RIF1 is poorly conserved and is characterized by a high degree of intrinsic disorder.
source: The region spanning between these N- and C-terminal motifs is poorly conserved and is characterized by a high degree of intrinsic disorder (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A showing the disorder profile plot.

claim: RIF1 contains multiple serine-glutamine/threonine-glutamine (SQ/TQ) motifs, which are consensus sites for phosphorylation by the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR.
source: Additionally, RIF1 contains multiple serine-glutamine/threonine-glutamine (SQ/TQ) motifs, which are consensus sites for phosphorylation by the DNA damage response kinases ATM and ATR (Blackford and Jackson, 2017; Figure 1A, Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work and Figure 1A.

claim: Activated B cells undergo a proliferative burst that renders them susceptible to DNA replication stress and damage.
source: In addition to experiencing programmed DSB formation and repair during Ig CSR, activated B cells undergo a proliferative burst that renders them susceptible to DNA replication stress and damage (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1B and established knowledge.

claim: Activated B cells express considerably higher levels of RIF1 than their mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) counterparts.
source: Furthermore, activated B cells express considerably higher levels of RIF1 than their mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) counterparts (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data in Figure 1C.

claim: Analysis of post-translationally modified RIF1 peptides from different I-DIRT preparations revealed phosphorylation to be the predominant PTM, with the majority of phosphoresidues being serines followed by either a proline or a glutamic acid (SP or SE).
source: Analysis of post-translationally modified RIF1 peptides from different I-DIRT preparations revealed phosphorylation to be the predominant PTM, with the majority of phosphoresidues being serines followed by either a proline or a glutamic acid (SP or SE) (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of mass spectrometry data.

claim: S1387Q, S1416Q, and S1528Q were reproducibly found to be phosphorylated across independent RIF1 I-DIRT datasets.
source: Among all SQ/TQ motifs present in mouse RIF1, S1387Q, S1416Q, and S1528Q were reproducibly found to be phosphorylated across independent RIF1 I-DIRT datasets (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: S1387Q, S1416Q, and S1528Q exhibit a relatively high degree of conservation across species.
source: These SQ motifs exhibit a relatively high degree of conservation across species (Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by sequence alignment data in source data files.

claim: S1387Q, S1416Q, and S1528Q are located in close proximity to each other and form a defined cluster of SQ sites in the IDR of both mouse and human RIF1.
source: More interestingly, S1387Q, S1416Q, and S1528Q (S1403Q, S1431Q, and S1542Q in hRIF1) are located in close proximity to each other and form a defined cluster of SQ sites in the IDR of both mouse and human RIF1 (IDR-CII SQs) (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1G showing the schematic representation of SQ/TQ motif clusters.

claim: Phosphorylation of residues within IDRs has been reported to affect protein functions in a variety of cellular contexts.
source: Phosphorylation of residues within IDRs has been reported to affect protein functions in a variety of cellular contexts (Bah and Forman-Kay, 2016; Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: CH12 is a well-characterized mouse B cell lymphoma line that recapitulates the molecular mechanism and regulation of CSR.
source: CH12 is a well-characterized mouse B cell lymphoma line that recapitulates the molecular mechanism and regulation of CSR (Nakamura et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: CH12 cells display a stable near-diploid genome that can be easily and efficiently manipulated by somatic gene targeting.
source: Furthermore, CH12 cells display a stable near-diploid genome that can be easily and efficiently manipulated by somatic gene targeting (Delgado-Benito et al., 2020; Delgado-Benito et al., 2018; Sundaravinayagam et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Targeted deletion of Brca1 exon 11 in mice results in the expression of a splice variant (BRCA1-Δ11) that preserves intact N-terminal RING finger domain and C-terminal BRCT repeats but lacks key motifs that are essential for BRCA1 functions.
source: Targeted deletion of Brca1 exon 11 in mice results in the expression of a splice variant (BRCA1- Δ11) that preserves intact N-terminal RING finger domain and C-terminal BRCT repeats but lacks key motifs that are essential for BRCA1 functions (Evers and Jonkers, 2006; Xu et al., 2001; Xu et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: BRCA1-Δ11-expressing B cells exhibit genome instability because of impaired HR but undergo CSR as proficiently as WT cells.
source: BRCA1-Δ11-expressing B cells exhibit genome instability because of impaired HR but undergo CSR as proficiently as WT cells (Bunting et al., 2010; Callen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PARPi increases the load of DNA replication-associated breaks, and in BRCA1-deficient backgrounds it triggers the accumulation of chromatid breaks and radial chromosomes.
source: PARPi increases the load of DNA replication-associated breaks, and in BRCA1-deficient backgrounds it triggers the accumulation of chromatid breaks and radial chromosomes (Farmer et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PARPi-treated Brca1mut CH12 cell lines accumulated chromatid breaks and radials with high frequency.
source: Analysis of metaphase spreads revealed that in contrast to control cells PARPi-treated Brca1mut CH12 cell lines accumulated chromatid breaks and radials with high frequency (Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by metaphase analysis data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: All Brca1mut cell lines displayed reduced viability in the presence of PARPi compared to their wild-type counterparts.
source: Accordingly, all Brca1mut cell lines displayed reduced viability in the presence of PARPi compared to their wild-type counterparts (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In-bulk targeting of RIF1 as well as of the up- and downstream pathway components 53BP1 and REV7, respectively, led to a significant rescue of viability in Brca1mut cells.
source: In-bulk targeting of RIF1 as well as of the up- and downstream pathway components 53BP1 and REV7, respectively, led to a significant rescue of viability in Brca1mut cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Brca1mutRif1-/- clonal derivatives exhibited reduced levels of chromosomal aberrations and a marked increase in viability after PARPi treatment compared to Brca1mut cells.
source: Furthermore, Brca1mutRif1-/- clonal derivatives exhibited reduced levels of chromosomal aberrations and a marked increase in viability after PARPi treatment compared to Brca1mut cells (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–D.

claim: Brca1mut CH12 cell lines were able to undergo stimulation-dependent CSR to levels comparable to WT CH12 cells.
source: Accordingly, Brca1mut CH12 cell lines were able to undergo stimulation-dependent CSR to levels comparable to WT CH12 cells (Figure 2E), whereas deletion of RIF1 in these cells dramatically impaired CSR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by CSR assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of RIF1 in Brca1mut cells dramatically impaired CSR.
source: Accordingly, Brca1mut CH12 cell lines were able to undergo stimulation-dependent CSR to levels comparable to WT CH12 cells (Figure 2E), whereas deletion of RIF1 in these cells dramatically impaired CSR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by CSR assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: All Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines accumulated chromatid breaks and radial chromosomes to the same levels as the control Brca1mut genotype.
source: All Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines accumulated chromatid breaks and radial chromosomes to the same levels as the control Brca1mut genotype (Figure 2G) and were as sensitive to the treatment (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by metaphase analysis data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines were as sensitive to PARPi treatment as control Brca1mut genotype.
source: All Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines accumulated chromatid breaks and radial chromosomes to the same levels as the control Brca1mut genotype (Figure 2G) and were as sensitive to the treatment (Figure 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by viability assay data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: Brca1mutRif1-/- cells exhibited the expected reduction in chromosomal aberrations and rescue of viability.
source: In contrast, Brca1mutRif1-/- cells exhibited the expected reduction in chromosomal aberrations and rescue of viability (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claim: Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines all switched proficiently from expressing IgM to IgA.
source: Whereas Brca1mutRif1-/- cells were, as expected, severely impaired in the process, Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines all switched proficiently from expressing IgM to IgA (Figure 2I).
evidence: This claim is supported by CSR assay data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Phosphorylation of the conserved IDR-CII SQ motifs is dispensable for physiological levels of CSR.
source: This finding indicates that phosphorylation of the conserved IDR-CII SQ motifs is dispensable for physiological levels of CSR.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the CSR data showing that Brca1mutRif1S→A cell lines switch proficiently.

claim: IR induced a marked phosphorylation of RPA32 in Brca1mutRif1-/- cells.
source: As expected, IR induced a marked phosphorylation of RPA32 in Brca1mutRif1-/- cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: Brca1mutRif1S→A cells were as proficient as controls in counteracting RPA32 phosphorylation following IR-induced DSBs.
source: In contrast, Brca1mutRif1S→A cells were as proficient as controls in counteracting RPA32 phosphorylation following IR-induced DSBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: RIF1 is recruited to stalled DNA replication forks where it protects nascent DNA from degradation by the DNA2 nuclease in a manner dependent on its interaction with protein phosphatase 1 (PP1).
source: RIF1 is recruited to stalled DNA replication forks where it protects nascent DNA from degradation by the DNA2 nuclease in a manner dependent on its interaction with protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) (Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016; Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: BRCA1 plays a protective role at DNA replication forks that is independent from RIF1.
source: BRCA1 plays a protective role at DNA replication forks that is independent from RIF1 (Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016; Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019; Schlacher et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Deletion of RIF1 severely impaired CSR.
source: As expected, deletion of RIF1 severely impaired CSR (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), whereas, in agreement with the findings from the BRCA1-deficient background (Figure 2I), CSR was not affected in Rif1S→A cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and CSR assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: CSR was not affected in Rif1S→A cell lines.
source: As expected, deletion of RIF1 severely impaired CSR (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), whereas, in agreement with the findings from the BRCA1-deficient background (Figure 2I), CSR was not affected in Rif1S→A cell lines (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by CSR assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Rif1S→A cells did not display the IR-induced RPA phosphorylation that was detectable in the absence of RIF1.
source: Furthermore, analogously to what we described in the Brca1mut setting (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), Rif1S→A cells did not display the IR-induced RPA phosphorylation that was detectable in the absence of RIF1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Both Rif1-/- and Brca1mut genotypes exhibited the expected fork degradation phenotype.
source: Both Rif1-/- and Brca1mut genotypes exhibited the expected fork degradation phenotype (Figure 3C), thus indicating that the protective pathways mediated by these factors are active also in CH12 cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Rif1S→A clonal derivatives showed increased degradation of stalled forks compared to controls and to the same levels observed in Rif1-/- cells.
source: Interestingly, Rif1S→A clonal derivatives showed increased degradation of stalled forks compared to controls and to the same levels observed in Rif1-/- cells (Figure 3C), thus suggesting that abrogation of these IDR-CII SQ phosphorylation events prevents RIF1 function at the forks.
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: RIF1 protective role at stalled forks is dependent on the ability of its interactor PP1 to dephosphorylate and inactivate DNA2, which in turn limits the nuclease-mediated processing of DNA replication forks.
source: RIF1 protective role at stalled forks is dependent on the ability of its interactor PP1 to dephosphorylate and inactivate DNA2, which in turn limits the nuclease-mediated processing of DNA replication forks (Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: DNA2i treatment rescued the fork degradation phenotype in all HU-treated Rif1S→A clonal derivatives.
source: Analogously to the result observed in Rif1-/- cells (Figure 3D; Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019), DNA2i treatment rescued the fork degradation phenotype in all HU-treated Rif1S→A clonal derivatives (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Rif1S1387A and Rif1S1416A cell lines were proficient in protecting stalled forks from degradation.
source: We found that while Rif1S1387A and Rif1S1416A cell lines were proficient in protecting stalled forks from degradation, Rif1S1528A cells exhibited a reproducible fork degradation defect (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Rif1S1528A cells exhibited a reproducible fork degradation defect.
source: We found that while Rif1S1387A and Rif1S1416A cell lines were proficient in protecting stalled forks from degradation, Rif1S1528A cells exhibited a reproducible fork degradation defect (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The fork degradation phenotype in Rif1S1528A cells was modest and did not recapitulate the severe defect of Rif1-/- and Rif1S→A cells.
source: However, the phenotype was modest and did not recapitulate the severe defect of Rif1-/- and Rif1S→A cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by DNA fiber assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Phosphorylation of S1528 contributes to, but is not sufficient for, fork protection.
source: Altogether, this data suggests that phosphorylation of S1528 contributes to, but is not sufficient for, fork protection, and that multiple phosphorylation events within the IDR-CII SQ cluster are responsible for RIF1's ability to protect nascent DNA under conditions of replication stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the single mutant analysis data.

claim: Multiple phosphorylation events within the IDR-CII SQ cluster are responsible for RIF1's ability to protect nascent DNA under conditions of replication stress.
source: Altogether, this data suggests that phosphorylation of S1528 contributes to, but is not sufficient for, fork protection, and that multiple phosphorylation events within the IDR-CII SQ cluster are responsible for RIF1's ability to protect nascent DNA under conditions of replication stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of single and triple mutant phenotypes.

claim: RIF1S→A mutant protein retains the ability to interact with PP1.
source: We found that RIF1S→A mutant protein retains the ability to interact with PP1, thus indicating that the abrogation of phosphorylation events in the conserved cluster does not have a major impact on RIF1-PP1 association (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: RIF1 and EdU co-localization increased upon HU treatment in control cell lines.
source: As expected (Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019), RIF1 and EdU co-localization increased upon HU treatment in control cell lines (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4B and citations to prior work.

claim: The HU-induced RIF1-EdU proximity signal was only modestly affected in Rif1S→A clonal derivatives.
source: In contrast, the HU-induced RIF1-EdU proximity signal was only modestly affected in Rif1S→A clonal derivatives (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Phosphorylation of the IDR-CII SQ cluster facilitates RIF1 interaction with stalled replication forks.
source: This data suggests that phosphorylation of the IDR-CII SQ cluster facilitates RIF1 interaction with stalled replication forks.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PLA data showing reduced RIF1-EdU proximity in Rif1S→A cells.

claim: S1416 was identified to be phosphorylated in an HU-dependent manner.
source: Interestingly, the only SQ site that was identified to be phosphorylated in an HU-dependent manner was indeed one of the three conserved motifs of the IDR-CII SQ cluster, S1416 (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: HU-induced phosphorylation of S1416 was reduced following treatment with ATM and, to a lesser extent ATR, inhibitors.
source: In addition, HU-induced phosphorylation of S1416 was reduced following treatment with ATM and, to a lesser extent ATR, inhibitors (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: S1542 in hRIF1 (which corresponds to S1528 in mouse RIF1) is an SQ site phosphorylated following treatment with the DNA polymerase inhibitor aphidicolin.
source: In support of this point, an independent proteomics analysis of hRIF1 isolated from Flp-In T-REx GFP-RIF1-L cells (Watts et al., 2020) identified S1542 (which corresponds to S1528 in mouse RIF1, see Figure 1—source data 2) as an SQ site phosphorylated following treatment with the DNA polymerase inhibitor aphidicolin, which also induces replication stress (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4E and citation to prior work.

claim: SQ motifs in the conserved cluster are phosphorylated following treatment with replication stress-causing agents.
source: Collectively, these results build on the initial identification of S1416 and S1528 in the RIF1 I-DIRT preparations (Figure 1E and F) and demonstrate that SQ motifs in the conserved cluster are phosphorylated following treatment with replication stress-causing agents.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple mass spectrometry datasets.

claim: Replication stress induces phosphorylation events within the IDR-CII SQ cluster that promote RIF1 recruitment to stalled replication forks and protection of nascent DNA.
source: Altogether, these findings suggest that replication stress induces phosphorylation events within the IDR-CII SQ cluster that promote RIF1 recruitment to stalled replication forks and protection of nascent DNA.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined data on phosphorylation, recruitment, and fork protection.

claim: Downregulation or inactivating mutations in DSB end protection factors confer resistance to PARP inhibitors in BRCA1-deficient tumors in mice and a patient-derived model.
source: On the one hand, downregulation or inactivating mutations in DSB end protection factors confer resistance to PARP inhibitors in BRCA1-deficient tumors in mice and a patient-derived model (Dev et al., 2018; Jaspers et al., 2013; Noordermeer et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Protection of DNA replication forks has recently been proposed as a mechanism for chemoresistance in the context of BRCA deficiency.
source: On the other hand, protection of DNA replication forks has recently been proposed as a mechanism for chemoresistance in the context of BRCA deficiency (Ray Chaudhuri et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: RIF1 plays at least two roles in the preservation of genome integrity during DNA replication: a genome-protective role in stabilizing nascent DNA at stalled but unbroken forks, and a potentially genome-destabilizing role in regulating DNA repair by opposing resection at DSBs.
source: RIF1 plays at least two, and to some extent conflicting, roles in the preservation of genome integrity during DNA replication: a genome-protective role in stabilizing nascent DNA at stalled but unbroken forks, and a potentially genome-destabilizing role in regulating DNA repair by opposing resection at DSBs.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data and discussion in the manuscript.

claim: The protection of newly replicated DNA at stalled forks occurs through PP1-induced DNA2 inactivation.
source: Both roles depend on RIF1's ability to control DNA processing, albeit on different DNA substrates and via independent mechanisms: the protection of newly replicated DNA at stalled forks through PP1-induced DNA2 inactivation (Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019), and the inhibition of DSB resection at collapsed forks via the 53BP1-triggered cascade (Chapman et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The inhibition of DSB resection at collapsed forks occurs via the 53BP1-triggered cascade.
source: Both roles depend on RIF1's ability to control DNA processing, albeit on different DNA substrates and via independent mechanisms: the protection of newly replicated DNA at stalled forks through PP1-induced DNA2 inactivation (Garzón et al., 2019; Mukherjee et al., 2019), and the inhibition of DSB resection at collapsed forks via the 53BP1-triggered cascade (Chapman et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Zimmermann et al., 2013), respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The identified PTMs occur within a cluster of conserved SQ motifs in the IDR of mammalian RIF1.
source: Interestingly, the identified PTMs occur within a cluster of conserved SQ motifs in the IDR of mammalian RIF1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: IDRs are stretches of sequences that do not adopt any stable, defined secondary or tertiary structures.
source: IDRs are stretches of sequences that do not adopt any stable, defined secondary or tertiary structures (Wright and Dyson, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: Proteins characterized by a high degree of intrinsic disorder rapidly transition between different folding states.
source: Proteins characterized by a high degree of intrinsic disorder rapidly transition between different folding states.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about IDRs.

claim: Phosphorylation of 53BP1 SQ/TQ motifs within its intrinsically disordered N-terminus is essential for the DNA damage-dependent recruitment of RIF1 to sites of damage and protection against DSB resection.
source: As a relevant example, phosphorylation of 53BP1 SQ/TQ motifs within its intrinsically disordered N-terminus is essential for the DNA damage-dependent recruitment of RIF1 to sites of damage and protection against DSB resection (Chapman et al., 2013; Di Virgilio et al., 2013; Escribano-Díaz et al., 2013; Feng et al., 2013; Silverman et al., 2004; Zimmermann et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Abrogation of replication stress-induced phosphorylation of a cluster of conserved SQ motifs in RIF1 IDR impairs its recruitment to stalled DNA replication forks and results in DNA2-mediated degradation of nascent DNA.
source: In this study, we showed that abrogation of replication stress-induced phosphorylation of a cluster of conserved SQ motifs in RIF1 IDR impairs its recruitment to stalled DNA replication forks and results in DNA2-mediated degradation of nascent DNA.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Orthologous IDRs exhibit molecular features that are crucial for function but do not translate into any noticeable similarity at the level of primary amino acid sequences.
source: Orthologous IDRs exhibit molecular features that are crucial for function but do not translate into any noticeable similarity at the level of primary amino acid sequences (Zarin et al., 2019; Zarin et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The IDR of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rif1 contains a cluster of seven SQ/TQ consensus motifs for the ATM/ATR yeast homologs Tel1/Mec1, some of which have been reported to be phosphorylated in vivo.
source: In this regard, the IDR of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Rif1 contains a cluster of seven SQ/TQ consensus motifs for the ATM/ATR yeast homologs Tel1/Mec1, some of which have been reported to be phosphorylated in vivo (Smolka et al., 2007; Sridhar et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Abrogation of phosphorylation at seven SQ/TQ sites in yeast Rif1 impaired DNA replication fork protection after treatment with HU.
source: Interestingly, a recent bioRxiv manuscript showed that abrogation of phosphorylation at these seven SQ/TQ sites in yeast Rif1 impaired DNA replication fork protection after treatment with HU (Monerawela et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a preprint manuscript.

claim: The identification of a cluster of SQ/TQ motifs whose phosphorylation influences fork protection in both mammalian and yeast RIF1 hints at an evolutionary conserved mechanism for the regulation of nascent DNA processing under conditions of DNA replication stress.
source: Although RIF1 IDRs exhibit low conservation across evolution, the identification of a cluster of SQ/TQ motifs whose phosphorylation influences fork protection in both mammalian and yeast RIF1 hints at an evolutionary conserved mechanism, and underlying molecular feature, for the regulation of nascent DNA processing under conditions of DNA replication stress.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of mammalian and yeast data.
